comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I’m Jaclyn, co-founder and CEO of Alsona.Alsona finds the companies that are in market right now, so you can reach them before your competitors even know they’re looking.We built it for people who do their own outbound and secretly hate it. We spent years watching people try to spam their way to pipeline, and what we noticed after analyzing THOUSANDS of campaigns is that the predictor of a booked meeting was need and TIMING. today.name: TK by Medium

TK is our new agentic notebook, built by people who love to write, for a world that now runs on words.Every AI tool you use gets better the more of your thinking it can read, so every word you write, even the messy ones, works on your behalf.Chat apps can help you research, but TK helps you write. Three simple steps level up your writing: craft, compound, create.1. Craft. Writing is thinking. Craft your best writing distraction free—no clutter and a TK agent that works inline so that you never have take your fingers off the keyboard.Pull ideas from an instant memory of all your words: voice memos from your walk, partial drafts, Granola notes, Claude research chats, anything you’ve ever written on Medium, and, yes, your old Bear or Obsidian vault. ---2. Compound. Every note makes the next one more useful.Deep thinking comes from building on what you’ve written before. The TK agent can remember, prompt next steps, and organize all your writing. today.name: Latch.ai
today.tagline: Automate complex accounting work without a single prompt
today.description: Latch is built for accountants buried in click-heavy close work. Instead of writing prompts, you do a task on screen and talk it through, including the parts no SOP captures: the three-day matching window, the rate you always override. Latch asks about the exceptions, then builds a sidekick that runs the task the same way every time, right in the tools you already use. When something doesn't fit, it stops and asks you. Every step is logged for review.

comments.text: Hi Product Hunt! I’m Stefan, co-founder and CEO of Latch.AI has come with a lot of big promises, and yet many of us still spend hours pointing and clicking: pulling reports, moving data between systems, checking one number against another. That kind of work looks easy to automate until you dig in and find the nuance underneath: the exceptions, the edge cases, the judgment calls nobody wrote down.I’ve built and sold two companies, and in both, some of our most capable people lost hours every week to exactly this kind of work. I started Latch to capture the nuance and free people to focus on the work that really matters.You show Latch how the work gets done, and it helps you see which parts are truly repeatable and where the gray areas are. The repeatable parts become sidekicks that run the same steps every time and stop to ask you when they hit a gap they can’t fill or a decision they shouldn’t make alone. The goal is to hand the tedium to a machine, so people can spend their time on the judgment calls and new ideas that move things forward.We started with accounting teams, because few processes have more nuance than the month-end close. The capture tool is where the magic happens. As you work, it records three streams: your narration, your screen, and your clicks and keystrokes. That’s how you get a working sidekick without ever writing a prompt or opening a coding agent.Try our free plan today. No credit card required.One question for you: if you had one recurring task you could hand over that would be done right, how impactful would it be for you?

today.tagline: Behavioral QA agents that use your product like customers do
today.description: Find the tests you didn’t know to write. Tell Wren what should work in plain English. Its QA agents try the paths your customers take, like going back to change an address halfway through checkout or retrying a failed payment. comments.text: Hey Product Hunt! I’m Tom, co-founder of Seldon. We built Wren because your entire test suite can pass and a customer can still find a bug five minutes after you ship.We’re an applied research lab in SF. Our team includes researchers from MIT and Berkeley and people who’ve built products at Meta and Spotify. We put people and agents in front of the same screens and study where their decisions differ. That got us interested in a QA problem. A test can tell you whether the route you scripted works. Customers get to pick their own route.How does Wren work?Give it a goal in plain English, like “a new teammate should be able to accept an invite and join the workspace.”Wren’s QA agents open your app and try different ways to reach that goal. One might open the invite while signed into the wrong account, switch accounts halfway through, and try the link again. You can test those paths without writing a separate script for each one.When something breaks, you get a recording and the steps to reproduce it. You can run Wren alongside your existing tests in CI.Who’s it for?We built Wren for engineering and QA teams, from startups shipping new features every week to enterprise teams with years of test coverage. One early team told us Wren saved them days of QA before a release.Try it on something you already testYour first 10 runs are free. I’d start with a flow your team already has a passing test for. Did Wren catch something your suite missed? I’d love to hear what happened. We’ll be here all day.

comments.text: Hi Product Hunt, I'm Sarath, maker of Co-Review.I build with a coding agent most days. Each diff looked fine. comments.text: Hey Product Hunt! I'm Amjad, co-founder of HoundDog.ai. Today we're launching ProtoMap.The problemAI coding agents are writing more of our code every day, and every line adds services, calls and fields that the next agent has to rediscover. In a large gRPC + Protobuf codebase, a simple question like "what breaks if I change this service, RPC or field?" sends an agent off to grep, find and read files across repos, trying to piece together relationships in code that often isn't even checked out on the developer's machine. That's slow and expensive, the answer is often incomplete, and it changes from one run to the next.How ProtoMap is different 🚀ProtoMap doesn't replace your coding agent. It gives your agent the context it is missing. A deterministic static-analysis engine maps every service, API and field across your monorepos and microservices, refreshes the map on every commit, and serves it to engineers in a web platform and to coding agents over MCP.🔹 Multi-hop service dependencies: see the blast radius of a change up to five hops out.🔹 Method dependencies: find who calls an RPC, plus every call site with its file location.🔹 Field dependencies: see which services and repos send or receive a field like credit_card.🔹 Code owners: see every inbound service, plus the maintainers and dependents to notify.🔹 Unused RPCs: find dead RPCs, orphaned calls, and proto messages declared differently in two repos.Because agents query the graph instead of re-reading code, the cost of an answer depends on the question, not on the size of your codebase. For one enterprise customer with a monorepo of millions of lines and a complex web of gRPC services, ProtoMap reduced the time and tokens required for change planning by 8×.Who is it for?Engineering teams running gRPC + Protobuf at scale, and the AI coding agents working alongside them.BenchmarkIn the gallery video, you’ll see two live Claude Code sessions (Opus 5.5, high effort) running side by side, given the same prompt at the same moment and recorded on one screen.The prompt:"We want to remove the RPC acme.documents.v1.DocumentQueryService/ResolveDocuments. Find every place in every repo that calls it, including indirect calls through helpers, method names built from strings, registries, or reflection, and give file:line and the calling service for each so we can migrate them."On this prompt, ProtoMap was 7× faster and 36× cheaper, and used 93× fewer tokens:■ Claude Code alone (no MCP): 6:01 · $14.44 · 24.5M tokens■ Claude Code + ProtoMap MCP: 0:50 · $0.40 · 262K tokensFor more detailed benchmarks across 20 prompts on 9 gRPC repositories, see our benchmark page: https://hounddog.ai/protomap-benchmark/Live DemoVisit https://hounddog.ai/videos/protomap-demo/ to see our live demo at MozFest, which includes querying the service graph in our web platform to track dependencies for services, APIs and fields across multiple hops, including callers, callees and call sites. The demo also walks through our detailed benchmarks.🔗 Get startedProtoMap is free to run on your machine: the self-hosted web platform and CLI scanner. When you're ready to roll it out org-wide, the Enterprise plan keeps the graph fresh across every repo, with CI scans on every pull request and GitHub, Bitbucket and GitLab integrations. Get started at https://github.com/hounddogai/protomap We'd love your feedback, especially from anyone managing a large gRPC codebase!

comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? Over the last year, wiring an agent to a tool got easy. MCP standardized the interface, and any agent can now call Gmail or Salesforce after an afternoon of work.But the tool call is only the surface. Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. Works with the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, LangChain, Google ADK, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, and Claude Code. You keep your framework and backend.Which of these five has slowed your agent down the most?

So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
